top_choice_rationale: P001 (Melitz and Helpman, firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting and foreign investment) changed what trade economists measure and how they evaluate policy. It moved the unit of analysis from the industry to the firm. Its selection and reallocation mechanisms have been checked against firm-level data in many countries for over two decades, and it has spread into industrial organisation and quantitative macro. Its main weakness is the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the credited list, and the parametric dependence of the welfare magnitudes. I judge that a citation centred on the mechanism can manage the boundary, and that the size and checkability of the change in knowledge outweigh cleaner credit. P002 (Grossman and Helpman) is a close second. It has the cleanest attribution and no maturity concern, but its protection-for-sale predictions are less consistently confirmed. P004 comes third for its credible design-based evidence, with the persistence debate and the task-strand attribution still open. P003 comes fourth because its identification is weaker and it sits close to the 2024 prize. All four are substantive awards, so I rank no award last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; no tie to Helpman, Melitz, Grossman, Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Persson, Tabellini or Besley. My Lund economic-history co-authors are not credited on any slate proposal. Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund; both are committee colleagues, not candidates.
